title: The Effect of Digital Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia in People With Co‐Morbid Insomnia and Sleep Apnoea (COMISA): A Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial

sections.abstract:
Co‐morbid insomnia and sleep apnoea (COMISA) is a prevalent and debilitating condition. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBTi) is an effective but largely inaccessible treatment in patients with COMISA. We aimed to test a self‐guided interactive digital CBTi program tailored for COMISA and insomnia alone. A pilot randomised controlled trial was conducted to investigate the effect of an interactive tailored digital CBTi program, versus digital sleep education (control) on symptoms of insomnia, depression, anxiety, sleepiness, fatigue, and maladaptive beliefs about sleep in people with COMISA. Online questionnaires were administered at baseline, 8 weeks, 16 weeks, and 24 weeks. Intent‐to‐treat mixed models and complete‐case Fisher's exact analyses were used. Participants were 30 adults with COMISA (Age M[sd] = 61.0[10.3], 60% female, BMI = 33.5[6.5]). Compared to control, CBTi was associated with lower insomnia ( M [95% CI] difference = 8.3[5.0–11.6], p < 0.001, d = 2.88), depression (3.7[1.0–6.5], p = 0.008, d = 1.66), anxiety (2.9[0.9–4.9], p = 0.005, d = 0.62), sleepiness (2.7[0.8–4.5], p = 0.007, d = 0.71), and maladaptive beliefs about sleep (13.9[5.7–22.2], p = 0.001, d = 1.16), but not fatigue (1.9[−1.2–4.9], p = 0.229, d = 0.68) at 8‐week follow‐up, controlling for baseline scores. The CBTi group experienced greater rates of insomnia remission (ISI < 8; 42%, vs. 0%, p = 0.012), and improvement (ISI reduction ≥ 6; 75% vs. 14%; p = 0.004) by 8‐weeks. Improvements in the CBTi group were sustained by 24‐weeks. This tailored digital CBTi program led to large and sustained improvements in insomnia, depression, anxiety, sleepiness, and maladaptive beliefs about sleep in people with COMISA.

Trial Registration: This trial was prospectively registered on the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR, ACTRN12622001218785). https://www.anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?id=384648&isReview=true

Keywords: COMISA, dCBTi, difficulties initiating and maintaining sleep, DIMS, OSA, sleep disordered breathing
sections.introduction:
Insomnia and obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are the two most prevalent sleep disorders and frequently co‐exist, resulting in impaired sleep, daytime function, and mental health (Sweetman et al. 2017 ). It is important to develop and implement effective treatment approaches for Co‐Morbid Insomnia and Sleep Apnoea (COMISA).

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBTi) is the recommended ‘first‐line’ treatment for insomnia (Riemann et al. 2023 ), and is effective in people with co‐morbid treated and untreated OSA (Sweetman et al. 2023 ). However, access to CBTi is extremely limited (Jernelöv and Blom 2023 ). To improve access to CBTi, therapist‐delivered programs have been translated to self‐guided digital programs (Soh et al. 2020 ; Zachariae et al. 2016 ). However, most digital CBTi programs have been developed for people with insomnia alone, and may not be as effective, safe, or suitable in those with COMISA. Therapist‐delivered CBTi programs in people with COMISA often include adaptations based on specific patient presentations (e.g., daytime sleepiness, OSA treatment/s, etc.), which may not occur in standard digital CBTi programs. Indeed, several clinical trials of existing digital CBTi programs have excluded people with suspected and confirmed OSA (Christensen et al. 2016 ; Espie et al. 2019 ; Nazem et al. 2023 ). In particular, there are concerns that CBTi may acutely increase risks of daytime sleepiness, attention lapses and functional impairment in people with COMISA, resulting in risks of side‐effects, or reduced engagement with treatment (Sweetman et al. 2020 ; Turner et al. 2022 ).

We therefore aimed to work with individuals with insomnia‐alone and COMISA to co‐design a self‐guided digital CBTi program, Bedtime Window, that provides tailored treatment for individuals experiencing either presentation. In a previous randomised controlled trial, we found that the program resulted in large and sustained improvements in insomnia, daytime function, and mental health symptoms in people with insomnia‐alone (Sweetman, Reynolds, and Richardson 2024 ). In a recent quasi‐experimental study, we reported that the program was associated with large and sustained improvements in insomnia, daytime function, and mental health symptoms in people with insomnia symptoms and suspected OSA (according to self‐reported OSA risk factors and symptoms) (Sweetman, Reynoldset, Lack, et al. 2024 ). However, participants with confirmed OSA were excluded from this study, and no control group was used. It is important to investigate the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of this tailored digital CBTi program in people with comorbid insomnia symptoms and a confirmed diagnosis of OSA with a randomised controlled trial.
sections.methods:
A pilot online RCT was conducted to compare the effect of tailored digital CBTi to digital sleep education (control) on symptoms of insomnia, depression, anxiety, fatigue, sleepiness, and maladaptive beliefs about sleep at 8‐week follow‐up in Australian adults with clinically significant insomnia symptoms and a previous diagnosis of OSA. Participants completed online screening, consent, and baseline questionnaires, before being randomised (1:1; computer generated randomisation sequence) to immediate CBTi or control. A questionnaire battery including standardised questionnaire measures of insomnia, depression, anxiety, fatigue, sleepiness, and maladaptive beliefs about sleep (See Supplement) was administered at baseline, 8‐week, 16‐week, and 24‐week post‐randomisation. The control group was provided access to the digital CBTi program after the 8‐week follow‐up. This study was approved by the Southern Adelaide Clinical Human Research Ethics Committee (2022/HRE00217), and registered on the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12622001218785). Recruitment ended after the intended sample of 30 participants was recruited.

Inclusion criteria were age ≥ 18, access to an internet‐compatible phone, tablet or computer, basic English language comprehension (to access the program), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) ≥ 15, and a self‐reported doctor diagnosis of OSA. Exclusion criteria were bipolar disorder, schizophrenia disorder, epilepsy, pregnancy, self‐reported risk of suicide and/or self‐harm (PHQ‐9, item 9 score ≥ 1), excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale score ≥ 16), current shift work, operating heavy machinery or driving for work, having a previous diagnosis of a cognitive impairment, doctor diagnosis of any sleep disorder other than insomnia or OSA, and any previous sleepiness‐related motor vehicle accident.

The tailored digital CBTi program, Bedtime Window, is described in previous publications (Sweetman, Reynolds, and Richardson 2024 ). The program assesses for insomnia symptoms, severity, and duration, and suspected/confirmed OSA and other sleep conditions at baseline, and adjusts treatment recommendations to balance therapeutic benefit while mitigating risks of daytime sleepiness and alertness‐failure. For example, based on users' sleep, wake and lifestyle information provided at baseline, a suite of underlying proprietary algorithms provide tailored recommendations to enact sleep restriction, regularisation, compression or extension therapies. Additional sleep, wake and lifestyle information provided by users during each weekly session and in daily sleep–wake diaries is additionally used by these algorithms to re‐evaluate and provide personalised recommendations to titrate bedtime recommendations during each session. Information about confirmed and suspected sleep apnoea, and symptoms of sleepiness at baseline and during each session is used to dynamically adjust treatment recommendations to incorporate sleep, wake, lifestyle, and daytime sleepiness parameters (and changes in these parameters over the course of treatment) such that risks to the patient are mitigated while treatment recommendations still result in effective treatment of insomnia. Interactive components are used throughout the program to maintain engagement and to assess and confirm understanding of different therapy concepts and recommendations. Immediately after completing each session, users receive a resource with personalised recommendations. Rates of session completion were used as a measure of adherence to the program. The control group received 5 weekly digital sleep education packets. Access to each weekly digital education packet was used as a measure of ‘adherence’ in the control group.

Data were analysed according to a pre‐defined Statistical Analysis Plan with SPSS Version 27 (IBM Corporation, Armonk NY, USA). A sample size requirement of 30 participants was based on a predicted 6‐point between‐group difference in the ISI at 8‐weeks (standard deviation = 4.5), accounting for 50% attrition. The statistical analysis approach is further described in the supplement.

A significant group by time interaction was observed from baseline to 8‐weeks for the ISI (Table 2 ). After adjusting for baseline scores, the CBTi group had lower ISI scores at 8‐weeks than the control group. The CBTi group experienced a large and statistically significant ISI reduction from baseline to 8‐weeks, and no subsequent change from 8‐weeks to 16‐weeks or 8‐weeks to 24‐weeks, indicating sustained improvement (Table 2 ). The control group experienced no significant change in the ISI from baseline to 8‐weeks, but a subsequent improvement in the ISI between 8‐weeks and 16‐weeks (i.e., after accessing the tailored digital CBTi program), that was sustained from 8‐weeks to 24‐weeks (Table 2 ).

Between‐group changes in estimated marginal mean ( ± 95% CI) questionnaire scores during the study.

Note : All analyses adjusted for baseline scores. Bold formatting indicates p values < 0.05.

Abbreviations: CBTi, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia; d , Cohen's d .

There was no between‐group difference in ISI scores at 16‐weeks or 24‐weeks, indicating similar levels of insomnia severity in both groups after they accessed the tailored digital CBTi program.

The same pattern was observed when examining the ISI nocturnal subscale and ISI daytime subscales (Table 2 ).

A similar pattern of between‐group differences favouring the CBTi group was observed for symptoms of depression, anxiety, sleepiness, and maladaptive beliefs at 8 weeks (See Table 2 and Supplement). There was no between‐group difference in symptoms of fatigue at 8‐week follow‐up (Table 2 , and Supplement).

The ESS was also completed during each weekly session of the tailored digital CBTi program. An intent‐to‐treat mixed model including peri‐treatment data collapsed across both groups indicated that there was no significant change in ESS scores from Session 1 to any subsequent session of the CBTi program (all p > 0.482).

A series of responder analyses were used to investigate between‐group differences in patterns of insomnia remission (ISI < 8), Normal/Mild insomnia (ISI < 15), and clinically meaningful important difference in insomnia (ISI reduction ≥ 6 (Yang et al. 2009 ), and ISI reduction ≥ 8) by 8 weeks (Table 3 ). Other than the ISI ≥ 8 point reduction criterion, greater rates of improvement/remission were consistently observed in the CBTi than control group across these criteria. Responder data are additionally reported at 16‐week and 24‐week follow‐up (although between‐group differences are not reported, as both groups had accessed the CBTi program).

Between‐group rates of insomnia remission, response, and minimum clinically important difference by 8‐week follow‐up.

Note : Fisher's exact p used due to low cell count criteria. Between‐group p values are not presented at 16‐weeks or 24‐weeks, as both groups had received CBTi.

Abbreviations: CBTi, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for insomnia; ISI, Insomnia Severity Index; MCID, minimum clinically important difference.

Upon completion of Session 5 of the program, participants were invited to provide feedback on the digital CBTi program. Of the 21 participants that completed the fifth session (data collapsed across both groups), 95% of participants indicated that the program was easy to use, 100% indicated that they acquired new knowledge during the program, and 100% indicated that they would recommend the program to a family member or friend.
sections.discussion:
This digital CBTi program tailored for COMISA and insomnia‐alone resulted in large and sustained improvements in symptoms of insomnia, depression, anxiety, sleepiness, and mal‐adaptive beliefs about sleep in people with COMISA. By post‐treatment, 92% of participants in the CBTi group reported insomnia symptoms in the Normal/Mild range, and 42% experienced insomnia remission. Average levels of daytime sleepiness did not increase significantly during any session of the program, and were significantly improved by 8‐weeks post‐randomisation.

The most common exclusion reasons were self‐reported risk of self‐harm/suicide risk, comorbid restless legs syndrome, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Consequently, this digital program has not been validated in the context of these comorbidities/symptoms, and CBTi delivered by clinicians with training and experience in CBTi delivery may be more appropriate. Among 43 potential participants with moderately severe insomnia symptoms, 30 were eligible and recruited to this study, while 13 were ineligible and directed to specialist care. Directing approximately 70% of people with COMISA (30/43 people) to an evidence‐based tailored digital CBTi program may reduce the burden on valuable clinician resources to manage the remaining 30% of people that require specialist care.

At baseline, all participants reported OSA diagnosed according to an overnight sleep study. Participants also reported symptoms of ‘moderately severe’ or ‘severe’ insomnia that had persisted for at least 3 months, consistent with a diagnosis of ‘chronic insomnia’ (AASM 2023 ). Most participants reported current insomnia symptoms despite using other management approaches for insomnia and OSA. Despite these other treatments, this program was associated with large improvements in insomnia and mental health symptoms within an 8‐week period that were sustained by 24‐week follow‐up. Consequently, these pilot data indicate that this program may be an effective and acceptable intervention in people with COMISA who are experiencing chronic insomnia symptoms that are resistant to other management approaches.

The lack of a significant between‐group difference in fatigue by 8 weeks appears to be largely due to the control group experiencing a similar improvement in daytime fatigue by 8 weeks. In a similar recent RCT in 62 people with insomnia alone, the CBTi group reported significantly greater improvement in daytime fatigue than the digital sleep education control group, who did not experience any change in fatigue symptoms by 8 weeks (Sweetman, Reynolds, and Lack, et al. 2024 ).

These pilot data are based on a sample of only 30 participants, and larger clinical trials are required to confirm these findings in different sub‐samples of people with COMISA and in different management settings. Furthermore, there were missing data for one participant in the control group and three participants in the intervention group at 8‐week follow‐up (representing a ~ 13% rate of 8‐week missing data). The proportion of missing 8‐week data is relatively low for an online intervention/study, and rates of missing data were not significantly different between groups. However, the amount of missing data is an important limitation when considering the small sample size of this study and highlights the need for larger studies in the future.

This study included participants with treated OSA and untreated OSA. This is because previous trials of digital CBTi have excluded both of these sub‐groups of people with COMISA, and we were interested in initially studying the effectiveness and acceptability of the program in a diverse sample of participants. A recent meta‐analysis reported that therapist‐administered CBTi is an effective treatment in the presence of treated and untreated OSA (Sweetman et al. 2023 ). Given the small sample size of this study, we did not investigate differences in treatment‐response between those with treated vs. untreated OSA.

We did not investigate ‘down‐stream’ impacts of CBTi on manifestations of OSA severity, or use of OSA treatments. This pilot study was powered to identify a between‐group difference in insomnia severity in people with COMISA, which we felt was necessary before investigating the effect of this tailored digital CBTi program on patterns of PAP use (or adherence to other treatment/s for OSA). It is possible that tailored digital CBTi may improve PAP use in people with COMISA that are naïve to PAP (Alessi et al. 2021 ; Sweetman et al. 2019 ), and those who have already been prescribed PAP therapy (Eldridge‐Smith et al. 2022 ).

This self‐guided interactive tailored digital CBTi program tailored for insomnia‐alone and COMISA was associated with large and sustained improvements in symptoms of insomnia, depression, anxiety, sleepiness, and unhelpful beliefs about sleep in participants with COMISA. The program was acceptable to participants and there was no increase in self‐reported symptoms of daytime sleepiness during any treatment session. Larger clinical trials are required to determine the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of this program in different samples of people with COMISA.
